e.t: Abdiou; Avthiu is a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears eleven times across nine verses, including occurrences in 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and Obadiah. The name is associated with named individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person identified must be determined from each passage’s context.

Athani is a proper name, referring to a named individual or other named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its meaning is simply the name “Athani.” In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:26. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s specific identity must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This word is a personal name, referring to Ailōn, also rendered Elon. It identifies people named Ailōn or Elon rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages in Genesis, Joshua, Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. Its precise reference is determined by the person named in each passage.

e.h: Unconquerable and Unable to Be Overcome
e.t: This adjective means “unconquerable”: not able to be defeated, subdued, or overcome. It describes someone or something that cannot be successfully conquered. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:19. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its central meaning remains clear: firm against attack or opposition and beyond the power of an adversary to defeat.

Amathi is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, and its English rendering remains “Amathi.” The name occurs in Genesis 10:18, 2 Kings 14:25, and Jonah 1:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide a further descriptive meaning. Its role in any particular passage must therefore be understood from that passage’s context.

This Greek LXX particle expresses possibility or an indefinite sense, often conveyed by “perhaps” or “ever.” It does not name a person, object, or action; instead, it helps qualify the statement around it. Its exact force depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic contribution is to leave something open, possible, or indefinite. The particle occurs 596 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it serves a recurring role across many kinds of sentences.

This adjective describes something that cannot be healed or cured—something incurable. It is used three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, including Esther and the books of Maccabees. Its basic sense concerns a condition beyond ordinary healing, whether the word describes a person, illness, or situation; the exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage. The meaning is plainly negative: healing is not possible or the condition cannot be remedied.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to give something back in return or to repay. It describes an action of returning what is owed, received, or due, rather than simply giving for the first time. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezekiel and Daniel. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea remains reciprocal giving: one thing is given back in response to another.

This adjective describes someone or something viewed with hatred or hostility. It can characterize a person, attitude, or relationship as opposed and unwelcome rather than friendly or favorable. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central meaning remains a description of hostility or being hateful.

This Greek verb means “exhaust”: to use something up, drain its supply, or leave it spent. It describes an action that brings available strength, resources, or contents to an end. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, in Judges and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being exhausted and the surrounding sentence.

“Defense” refers to a spoken or presented case made to answer an accusation, charge, or question. As a noun, this word names the act or statement by which someone seeks to justify a position or respond for himself or others. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, at Wisdom 6:10. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central idea is a formal answer offered in one’s own support.

This Greek LXX verb means “put away” or “put off”: it describes removing, setting something aside, or placing it away. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and later writings. The surrounding sentence determines whether the action concerns an object, clothing, or something being removed from consideration.

This noun means “silversmith,” a person who works with silver. It identifies an occupation rather than a character trait, event, or spiritual status. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “silversmith,” showing a consistent and specific meaning. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself points to someone whose skilled work involves silver.

This word means “self-will; wilfulness”—the determined insistence on one’s own desires or decisions. It is a noun describing a quality or disposition rather than an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 24:8. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this quality functions in that particular passage.

Baalthamar, also rendered Vaalthamar, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a specific name in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in Judges 20:33. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its particular role in that passage cannot be explained further. The name itself should therefore be understood as a location or named entity identified by the passage, not as a common noun with a broader everyday definition.

This word is a proper name rendered “Barsamite” or “Varsamitis.” It identifies a person by name or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:31. The name alone does not explain the person’s role or significance; those details must come from the surrounding verse and passage. Its precise reference therefore depends on reading the passage where this name appears.

This proper name refers to a person from Bethlehem—a Bethlehemite. It identifies someone by connection with that town rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in 1 Samuel 16:18. Its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a designation for someone associated with Bethlehem.

This noun means "intention"—what someone has decided, purposed, or aims to do. It refers to an inward plan or deliberate purpose rather than a mere passing thought. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. The surrounding wording determines whose intention is meant and how that purpose relates to the action being discussed. Its basic sense remains the settled aim or purpose behind a person’s words or deeds.

Gazmoth is a proper name, functioning as the personal or identifying name “Gazmoth” rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:42. The available wording preserves the name itself and does not provide additional information about its meaning or the individual connected with it. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and genealogical context.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Gennēsar,” also given as “Yennisar.” It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name preserved in the Greek LXX tradition. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 11:67. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise contextual significance cannot be stated beyond identifying the named entity. This noun refers to torch-bearing or the light produced by torches. It describes the use or presence of torches rather than a person, object, or action unrelated to illumination. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning centers on carrying torches or torchlight. The word therefore points to visible illumination provided by hand-held flames.

This noun refers to a reservoir or tank, a place designed to hold a supply of water or another liquid. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Exodus and once in Baruch. Its basic meaning remains concrete and practical, describing a storage place rather than the liquid itself. The surrounding verse is needed to determine what kind of reservoir or tank is intended in either occurrence.

This adjective describes something as “belonging to the people; public”—something associated with the community rather than a private individual. Its central idea is what is shared by, connected with, or intended for the people. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether the emphasis falls on public status or belonging to the people in a particular sentence.

This noun means “interchange” or “exchange”: a mutual giving, receiving, or changing between parties. It points to something moving from one side to another rather than a one-sided act. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The word should therefore be understood as describing reciprocal transfer or substitution, with the precise application determined by the sentence in which it appears.

This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “seventy times”. It describes the number of times something happens, emphasizing a repeated action counted to seventy. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 4:24. The word itself gives a precise numerical measure, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific action or situation being counted. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: it marks repetition occurring seventy times, rather than merely indicating an indefinite or large number.

Edrai, also rendered Ethre, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Samuel 6:17 and once in 1 Kings 2:46. The available information identifies it as a personal or place name, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to determine which. Its precise reference therefore depends on the passage where it appears.

e.h: Run Out or Make a Sally
e.t: This verb means “run out” or “make a sally,” describing movement outward from a place or position. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 11:36. Its central idea is leaving a position to move outward, with “make a sally” suggesting an outward advance or sortie. The precise force in that sentence depends on its surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. The word is therefore best understood as an action of going out rather than remaining in place.

This verb means to “sober up”: to come out of an intoxicated or impaired state and regain clear awareness. It describes a change into sobriety rather than merely naming a sober condition. Within this LXX corpus, it occurs six times across several passages, showing that this basic sense is used in more than one setting. The exact emphasis in any particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw out”: to pull something from within or remove it by force. It can describe physically extracting something, such as pulling prey from an animal, or bringing something out from a place. The same basic idea applies whether the object is a weapon, a person, or something held inside. It occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 17 verses, so its central sense remains consistent while the surrounding context identifies what is being drawn out.

Elphaal, also rendered Elfaal, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:18, identifying a person in a genealogy. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to distinguish this individual from others, not to express a broader concept. The name’s precise significance is not defined by the available lexical information.

This word means “my,” expressing that something belongs to, comes from, or is closely associated with the speaker. It is a pronoun used to identify the speaker’s possession or connection, as in “my” house, “my” people, or “my” words. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 387 times, so it is a common way to mark personal relationship or ownership. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the noun or statement it accompanies.

Enach, also rendered Enakh, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in Numbers: 13:22 and 13:28. The name itself identifies a particular person or people-group in those passages; its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse text. This LXX form should be understood as a name, not expanded into an additional meaning beyond “Enach” or “Enakh.”

This word means “ornament,” referring to something that adorns or beautifies. It is a noun used for an item of decoration rather than an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in Song of Songs 4:9. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and specific: an ornament or adornment. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself carries this clear meaning.

This Greek LXX verb means “fully shapen; formed.” It describes something brought into a complete or definite shape rather than left unfinished. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 21:22–23. Its normal sense is the act or result of shaping something into a formed condition. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains completion of form.

This verb means “governor of,” describing someone who exercises authority over a place, people, or responsibility. It presents governing as an action rather than naming the office itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Judges 20:33 and Esther 3:13. Those references identify its limited distribution, while the basic meaning remains the act of governing or exercising oversight over what has been placed under a ruler’s authority.

This noun means “stretching,” describing an extension or drawing out. It presents the idea of something being lengthened, intensified, or extended rather than remaining in a settled condition. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only twice, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the act or condition of stretching. [p03:word:lxx:L705293:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705293:occurrences]

This word is a proper name: Eumenes, also rendered Evmenis. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or spiritual concept. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees—at 2 Maccabees 12:31 and 13:26. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish that person’s role, character, or actions. Its ordinary function is simply to designate the individual named Eumenes or Evmenis.

This Greek LXX noun means “purpose”: an intended aim or reason behind an action. It identifies what someone is seeking to accomplish, rather than describing the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 17:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the purpose or aim being pursued.

This Greek LXX noun means “sweet savour” or “sweetness,” describing something pleasing in its scent or taste. It is a word for a pleasant quality rather than an action or person. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Exodus 30:34. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the substance being mentioned. Its basic meaning remains a pleasing sweetness or fragrant pleasantness.

Tharthan is a proper name, referring to a particular person named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 18:17. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry can identify the name and its grammatical function, but it cannot responsibly explain the person’s role or the event in that verse.

Thobel, also rendered Thovel, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general concept; it identifies a named entity in the passages where it occurs. The name appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament, across eight verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function remains a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word.

Iabis, also rendered Iavis, is a proper name used for a person or place in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe a quality, action, or general object; it identifies a particular named subject. The name occurs 23 times across 20 verses in the Greek Old Testament, with occurrences in Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding passage, since the same name can identify a location or a person in different contexts.

Iarimouth is a personal name, also rendered as “Iarimuth.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:6. Because it is a proper name and no further lexical definition is given, its meaning is simply its role as the designation of that person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the individual’s place in that passage.

This word is the proper name “Hierōnymos,” identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal name in the Greek LXX corpus, not as a general vocabulary term with a broader everyday definition. It occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:2. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific role or significance there.

Ithamar is a personal name used to identify a particular person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears 22 times in this LXX corpus, across 21 verses, from Exodus through Ezra. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: when readers encounter Ithamar, they are being directed to a person named Ithamar. The surrounding passage is needed to understand that person's role in any particular verse.

Isai, also rendered Ise, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:14. By itself, the name identifies someone rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s specific role in the genealogy or account. The name should remain distinct from other similarly rendered names unless the surrounding Scripture establishes a connection.

This Greek LXX verb means “scatter” or “pour upon.” It describes an action in which something is dispersed or poured over something else. The word functions as a verb, so it expresses an act rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Exodus 24:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the spreading or pouring of something upon another.

This Greek LXX verb means “shoot down with a bow.” It describes using a bow to strike and bring down a target, emphasizing an attack carried out by archery. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, 2 Kings, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the deliberate shooting down of someone or something with a bow.

This noun means an edict or proclamation: an officially announced message intended to be heard and acted upon. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to a public declaration rather than a private conversation. The word occurs three times in the LXX, in 2 Chronicles, Proverbs, and Jonah, and is rendered “proclamation” where English rendering is available. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the central idea remains an authoritative announcement made publicly.

This Greek LXX noun means “top” or “summit,” referring to the highest part of something, such as the top of a mountain or another elevated place. It can describe a physical peak or uppermost point. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, with both “top” and “summit” expressing its central sense. Its precise force in any verse depends on what place or object is being described.

This word means a “vegetable garden” or “kitchen garden”—a cultivated place where vegetables and other food plants are grown. It refers to land made productive by human care, rather than wilderness or uncultivated ground. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 11:10. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular comparison or emphasis in that passage; the word itself names the cultivated garden.

This verb means “fall into a swoon” or “faint”—to lose strength or consciousness. It describes a person becoming overwhelmed physically to the point of collapsing or passing out. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 4 Maccabees 6:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central meaning is the act of fainting rather than a lasting condition.

Maan is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, used to identify a specific named entity rather than describe an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is simply the name “Maan”; the available lexical information does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another particular entity. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, across five verses, from Joshua 21:34 through 1 Samuel 25:2. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “that which is learnt” or a “lesson”—something received or gained through learning. It refers to an acquired teaching or piece of knowledge rather than to the act of learning itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 13:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a lesson or learned matter.

This verb means to be or act “high-minded,” describing a person’s elevated or noble frame of mind. It functions as an action word rather than a name for a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:24. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here; its basic lexical sense remains the quality or action of being high-minded.

This Greek verb means “come,” describing movement toward a place or arrival. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, where the surrounding sentence determines who is coming and where the movement is directed. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, across six verses, including passages in 1 Samuel, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its basic sense remains straightforward: someone or something comes, arrives, or approaches. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, identifying Medaba, also given as Mithava. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:36. Because the verse text is not included here, its specific historical significance cannot be stated beyond its naming function. It should therefore be read as a name rather than as a general description or action word in that passage.

Mōphaz, also rendered Mofaz, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a person or place by name within the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Jeremiah 10:9. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific referent must be determined from that passage itself.

This noun means “fasting,” the practice or condition of going without food. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Daniel 6:19, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word names fasting itself rather than describing a person, action, or place. Its precise force in Daniel depends on the sentence and passage where it occurs.

Ozouz, also rendered Ozuz, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 5:8. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily its role in identifying the named individual or entity in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context. The name itself does not provide a broader concept or instruction for readers.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “diminish”: it describes something becoming less or being reduced. It can express decline in size, strength, number, influence, or degree, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 11 times across 11 Old Testament verses in the Greek Septuagint, so its basic sense is consistent while its exact application depends on the surrounding context. It is used in passages from Judges, Kings, Psalms, Proverbs, Joel, and other books.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something made from solid metal that has been beaten or hammered into shape. It emphasizes the material and sturdy construction of the object rather than its color, decoration, or purpose. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Sirach 50:9, and its basic meaning is “made of solid beaten metal.” Its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the adjective itself points to a durable metal object formed by hammering.

This word means “together,” describing people, things, or actions joined in one place, group, or shared circumstance. It functions as an adverb or adjective, helping show that something happens collectively rather than separately. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, with most occurrences in the deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense remains the idea of being united or present with others, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is joined together. It is found from Job through 4 Maccabees.

Ouphi, also rendered Ufi, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea, but a personal name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 34:23. Its precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding passage, since the name itself supplies a designation rather than a broader definition.

This Greek LXX verb means “press”: to urge someone strongly or persist in asking until action is taken. It describes forceful insistence rather than simple invitation. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament, in scenes involving people being urged, persuaded, or pressed to respond. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on who is pressing and how the surrounding passage describes the response.

This adjective means “fivefold”: it describes something marked by five or by a five-part quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 6:31. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided, the word’s exact referent cannot be described here; its lexical sense remains the simple idea of being fivefold. It functions as a descriptive adjective.

This noun means “surrounding land” or “that which surrounds.” It refers to the land around a city or designated place, rather than the central location itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 63 times, especially in descriptions of the lands assigned around Israelite cities and towns. The word therefore helps distinguish a settlement from its surrounding territory. Its exact force in any verse depends on the place and land being described.

This Greek LXX noun means “boat,” referring to a vessel used on the water. It names a physical means of travel or transport, rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for watercraft across this corpus. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “drinking,” referring to the act or practice of taking liquid. It names the activity itself rather than a particular drink. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 39 times, so its basic sense is used across a range of passages involving ordinary liquid consumption. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to drinking as an action, a practice, or part of a larger setting. Its core meaning remains straightforward: the act of drinking.

This verb describes being first in wronging someone—that is, taking the first step in treating another person unjustly. It focuses on who initiates the wrongdoing, rather than merely describing the existence of wrong. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 18:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of being first to wrong another.

This verb means “continue on”: it describes ongoing action rather than a completed or stopped action. As a verb, it tells what someone or something continues to do. Within this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. The particular object or activity being continued must be understood from the surrounding verse. Thus, its basic meaning is forward continuation, not a separate name or object.

This word means “morning”. It refers to the early part of the day, when daylight begins. It can function as a noun for that time or as an adjective describing something associated with morning. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 10 times, most often in Psalms, with additional occurrences in books such as 2 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on the beginning of the day rather than on a particular event or spiritual idea.

This noun means a pyramid, referring to a large, pyramid-shaped structure. It names a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 13:28. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the structure in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, which is not included here.

Razis, also written Rhazis, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, the name occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 14:37. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself establishes the person’s identity but does not by itself explain his actions or significance in that account. Its ordinary meaning is therefore simply the personal name Razis or Rhazis.

This verb means “snore”: to make the characteristic sound of heavy or sleeping breathing. It describes an audible action rather than a person’s identity or a spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Jonah 1:5–6, so its meaning is focused and concrete. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular scene, but the word itself simply refers to snoring.

Seera is a proper name, also rendered “Sira,” identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. This name appears once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 7:24. Its precise significance beyond identifying the named person cannot be determined from the available lexical information alone; the surrounding verse and passage would be needed for further explanation.

This verb means to wear a wreath, describing someone who has a wreath placed or displayed upon the head. It presents the act of wearing the wreath rather than naming the wreath itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 4:2. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains the act of wearing a wreath.

This verb means “hate” or “abominate,” expressing strong rejection or deep hostility toward someone or something. As a verb, it describes treating its object with intense aversion rather than merely disliking it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in 2 Maccabees 5:8 and once in 3 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “burn up”: to consume something with fire or intense heat. It describes the action of burning rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, showing a recurring description of heat or destruction by burning. Its central idea remains straightforward wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines what is being burned and how the action functions in that passage.

This noun means “valuation” or “assessment”: the act or result of determining the worth of a person, object, or obligation. It refers to an assigned value rather than to the thing being valued. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, chiefly in Leviticus, Numbers, and 2 Kings, where matters of value or financial reckoning are addressed. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Tanach” or “Tanakh.” It functions as a name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or ordinary object. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times: once in Numbers and twice in Joshua. The available renderings preserve the name as “Tanach,” so its central meaning is the designation itself rather than a broader translated concept. gl: hole formed by gnawing; mouse's hole

e.t: This word refers to a hole formed by gnawing, especially a mouse’s hole. It is a noun describing a physical opening or hollow space made in this way. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages associated with 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, Job, and Isaiah. The basic idea remains concrete and local: a small cavity or hiding place cut into the ground, wall, or another surface by gnawing.

This word means “water jar,” a container used to carry or hold water. It is a noun naming the vessel itself, not the water inside it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 18 times across 17 verses, showing a practical object used in ordinary scenes involving drawing, carrying, or keeping water. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 24, and its final occurrence is in Ecclesiastes 12:6. The surrounding passage determines the particular role the jar has in each verse, but the word’s basic meaning remains a water jar.

This word describes someone who is proud—exalting himself or holding an elevated opinion of himself rather than walking humbly. It can function as an adjective describing a person or attitude, and as a noun referring to such a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 39 times, including passages in Job and Psalms where “proud” is the established English rendering. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “remembrance” or “memorial”—something connected with keeping a person, event, or matter in memory. It refers to a reminder or memorial record rather than an action or feeling. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in 2 Samuel and once in Ezra. Its basic sense remains focused on preserving something in memory so that it can be recalled or remembered. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what serves as the remembrance or memorial in each passage.

This noun means the use of drugs or spells. It describes practices involving substances or spell-casting, with the surrounding passage indicating which sense is intended. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs eight times, appearing in Exodus, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its meaning remains focused on these practices rather than serving as a general term for every kind of wrongdoing.

Phasodomin, also rendered Fasothomin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:13. Its precise referent must therefore be established from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “corrupt”: to spoil, damage, or bring something into a ruined condition. It describes a change from what is sound or whole to what has been harmed or made defective. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it can describe corruption in more than one setting. Its basic sense remains the same whether the corruption concerns a thing, a condition, or what has been morally spoiled. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

To roast means to cook something with heat, especially by exposing it directly to fire or intense heat. This word is a verb describing that action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, at Leviticus 2:14 and 23:14. Its ordinary sense remains focused on preparing something by roasting; the surrounding verse determines the specific object and purpose involved.

This noun means “widowhood,” the condition or state of being a widow. It refers to life after the death of a husband, emphasizing the person’s altered marital state rather than naming the widow herself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in Micah. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the condition of widowhood.

Choloub, also given as Kholuv, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which one. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:26. Its precise significance there depends on the verse and surrounding passage, which are not included here.

This word is a proper name referring to a person called “Ōbēd” or “Ovith.” It identifies someone rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 14 times, with occurrences in Ruth, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The name appears especially often in 1 Chronicles, but its basic function remains consistent: it serves as the personal name Obed in Old Testament passages.
